title: Turning a superconducting diode into a Feynman ratchet to realize a nanoscale heat engine
authors: Konstantinos Kontogeorgiou, İnanç Adagideli, Géraldine Haack, Fabian Hassler
abstract: Feynman's ratchet illustrates how work can be extracted from thermal fluctuations in the presence of two heat baths at different temperatures. While some experimental realizations of the ratchet effect have been studied, most lack miniaturization, which is important for some applications. Here, we propose a physical implementation of Feynman's ratchet based on Josephson junctions exhibiting the superconducting diode effect. This setup functions as a heat engine that generates work solely from a temperature gradient via thermal fluctuations. We analyze its output power and efficiency, and, through the Seebeck coefficient, identify the conditions under which the device operates in reverse, functioning instead as a Peltier cooler.
summary: This theoretical work proposes using a superconducting diode as a physical realization of a Feynman ratchet to build a nanoscale heat engine. By exploiting the diode's asymmetry and coupling it to a temperature gradient, the device generates work from thermal fluctuations. The analysis confirms its function as a heat engine and demonstrates its ability to operate in reverse as a Peltier cooler.
main_problem: The paper aims to realize a nanoscale heat engine by converting thermal energy into mechanical work using a superconducting diode acting as a Feynman ratchet.
main_result: The setup successfully functions as a heat engine generating work solely from a temperature gradient, and it can also operate in reverse as a Peltier cooler.
method: The dynamics are analyzed using Langevin equations to model the superconducting phases coupled to two thermal reservoirs at different temperatures.
model_or_system: The physical system is a superconducting circuit incorporating a superconducting diode (modeled by Josephson junctions) coupled to two reservoirs at $T_1$ and $T_2$. The dynamics are governed by coupled Langevin equations.
key_observables: Output power ($\dot{W}$), efficiency ($\eta$), open-circuit voltage ($V_1$), and the Seebeck coefficient ($S$).
important_parameters: Temperature gradient ($\Delta T = T_2 - T_1$), coupling strength ($\kappa$), and external current ($I_{	ext{ext}}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a small effective inductance ($V_1 \approx V_2$) and that noise sources follow Gaussian distributions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the circuit setup, the dependence of heat engine efficiency ($\eta$) on the hot reservoir temperature ($T_2$), and the reversal of heat flow when operating as a cooler.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the physical model and the Feynman ratchet concept, develops the theoretical framework using Langevin equations, analyzes the steady-state operation for heat engine work extraction, and finally examines the reverse operation as a Peltier cooler.
why_interesting: The work bridges concepts from non-equilibrium statistical mechanics (Feynman ratchets) with solid-state quantum phenomena (superconducting diodes), providing a concrete, tunable model for energy conversion driven by thermal gradients.

FIG. 2. Open-circuit voltage is shown in units of V0 = I0R, while the temperature T1 of the ‘cold’ reservoir is given in units of T0 = EJ/kB. The values of the ‘hot’ reservoir tem- perature T2 are indicated in the inset. The coupling strength is fixed at κ = ℏ2/(4e2EJLeff) = 0.1 for all curves. Panel (a) demonstrates that for T2 ≲2.3T0, the maximum voltage occurs at finite T1, whereas for T2 ≳2.3T0, the maximum is reached at T1 →0 [panel (b)]. The blue curve for T2 = 6T0 and T1 = 0 marks the overall maximum voltage V1 = 0.045V0 attainable at κ = 0.1.

FIG. 3. Open-circuit voltage is shown in units of V0 = RI0, and the cold-reservoir temperature T1 is given in units of T0 = EJ/kB. The values of the dimensionless coupling constant κ are indicated in the inset. The hot-reservoir temperature is fixed at T2 = 5T0 for all curves. Panel (a) shows that for κ ≲0.04, the maximum voltage occurs at finite T1, whereas for κ ≳0.04 the maximum shifts to T1 →0, see panel (b). For consistency, the case κ = 0 is also included, where the voltage vanishes as expected.

FIG. 4. (a) Circuit voltage in units of V0 = RI0 as a function of Iext in units of I0. The circuit parameters are κ = 0.1, T2 = 2.3T0 and T1 = 0. This panel demonstrates that the dependence of the voltage as a function of the external applied current is linear in our regime. The point of maximum power is given for the values of Iext in which the voltage takes half of its maximum value. (b) Heat flow when operated as a heat engine: the lower and upper branches of the circuit are presented respectively as hot and cold reservoirs. The circuit works as a heat engine, extracting the heat −Q2 from the hot reservoir, delivering Q1 to the cold reservoir while producing the work W = −Q1 −Q2.

FIG. 5. Panel (a) shows the heat-engine efficiency η as a func- tion of the hot-reservoir temperature T2, given in units of T0, for different values of the coupling strengths κ. The maxi- mal efficiency is denoted by ηmax. As the coupling strength increases, the efficiency decreases. At the same time, the tem- perature T2 at which the efficiency reaches its maximum shifts toward lower values. This behavior is further illustrated in panel (b), which shows the corresponding cold-reservoir tem- perature T1 at maximum efficiency, also in units of T0.
